meta.blurb: Ines sells plants at a small Saturday market and has never been sure about her prices. With her nephew Theo she spends a year learning how people really judge a price, and how to use that honestly.
meta.bible: Ines: owner of a small plant stall at a Saturday market, warm, hardworking and honest. Theo: her nephew, 16, who studies Psychology and keeps the Notebook of tallies. Mrs Dale: an elderly regular customer in a green coat. The story runs over one year, from one Saturday to the next autumn. All money is in plain dollars. Prices in the story are imagined examples. Key terms: Anchor, Anchoring, Compromise effect, Decoy effect, Zero price, Pain of paying, Mental accounting, Bundle, Charm price, Reference price, Loss aversion, Framing, Choice overload, Endowment effect, Scarcity, Drip pricing, Pay what you like. The effects described are real and well studied, but several are not found in every study, and the book says so. No invented numbers or studies. Voice: warm, clear, practical and kind. The ethical rule of the book is to use these ideas to help people choose, never to trick them.

beats.scene: Ines arranges potted plants on a market stall with handwritten price cards
beats.summary: Ines sells plants at a Saturday market but is unsure about her prices.

beats.scene: Theo, a teenager in an apron, holds up a price card for Ines
beats.summary: Her nephew Theo helps on Saturdays and asks how she chose her prices.

beats.scene: Theo and Ines sit on upturned crates with a notebook between them
beats.summary: Theo says a price is also a message, and they decide to study prices for a year.

beats.scene: A customer compares two pots of different sizes on a wooden table
beats.summary: People rarely know what a plant is worth, so they judge by comparison.

beats.scene: A tall palm marked 60 stands behind medium ferns marked 25
beats.summary: Anchoring: the first number we see pulls our idea of a fair price towards it.

beats.scene: A customer reads the asking price on a card while Theo points at it
beats.summary: Even experts seem to be pulled by an anchor, so nobody is immune.

beats.scene: Ines looks proudly at her best palm and a small price card
beats.summary: Ines decides that an anchor must be honest: the palm must really be worth its price.

beats.scene: Mint plants in small, medium and large pots on a wooden table
beats.summary: Offered three sizes, many people choose the middle one: the compromise effect.

beats.scene: Theo marks a tally beside small, medium and large basil pots
beats.summary: Adding a plainly worse middle option can make the large one look better: the decoy effect.

beats.scene: Ines crosses out a price card and writes a new clear label
beats.summary: Ines decides that every option she sells must be a real choice that helps the customer.

beats.scene: A basket of seed packets stands beside plants under a sign reading Free
beats.summary: A price of zero feels special, so a free gift delights people.

beats.scene: A crowd gathers round free plant cuttings while a paid table stays quiet
beats.summary: Free attracts crowds but not always buyers, so a free gift should lead somewhere.

beats.scene: A customer taps a card on a small reader while holding a plant
beats.summary: Paying by card hurts less than cash, so people tend to spend a little more.

beats.scene: A woman with a gift card chooses a large orchid with a smile
beats.summary: People keep mental boxes for money, and gift money feels lighter than wages.

beats.scene: A man points at a small plant, then at a large tree behind it
beats.summary: Five dollars feels big against a small price and tiny against a large one.

beats.scene: Three small herb pots tied together with string and a price tag
beats.summary: Selling three items together as a set makes buying feel like one easy choice.

beats.scene: A gift set of plant, soil and care card in a paper bag
beats.summary: People pay more for a gift set that is ready to give, because it saves time and thought.

beats.scene: Two bottles of plant food, one marked three dollars, one marked six
beats.summary: When people cannot judge quality, a higher price can signal better quality, and a very low one can raise doubt.

beats.scene: Ines writes 19 on a card instead of 20 beside a pot
beats.summary: Prices that end in nine can feel much cheaper because people read the first digit most.

beats.scene: A tall orchid in a gift box labelled with a round price of 60
beats.summary: Round prices tend to suit things bought with feeling, and exact prices things bought for use.

beats.scene: A card showing a crossed-out price of 30 and a new price of 24
beats.summary: A sale works because the old price is a reference, so the old price must be real.

beats.scene: A sign reading Cash discount stands beside the card machine
beats.summary: Losses hurt more than gains please us, so a cash discount feels better than a card fee.

beats.scene: Customers stare at a long crowded table of forty different plants
beats.summary: Too many choices can freeze some shoppers, although studies disagree.

beats.scene: Three pots of one plant in different sizes, each with a clear card
beats.summary: Three clearly different sizes help every customer find the one that suits them.

beats.scene: Customers frown at a high price on watering cans on a hot sunny day
beats.summary: People judge prices by fairness, so raising a price when people are desperate can lose their trust.

beats.scene: Ines pins a small handwritten note about new prices to the stall
beats.summary: A price rise is accepted more easily when the reason is explained.

beats.scene: A delivery slip with an added fee surprises a puzzled customer
beats.summary: Hidden fees added at the last step make buyers feel tricked, so show the full price at the start.

beats.scene: Mrs Dale, an elderly regular in a green coat, fills her bag with plants
beats.summary: Honest, steady prices build the trust that brings customers back.

beats.scene: Ines adds up the cost of pots, soil, fuel and hours on a notepad
beats.summary: A price must first cover all costs, including her own time.

beats.scene: A rare spotted plant on a small stand attracts a keen collector
beats.summary: Costs set the lowest sensible price, but value to the customer sets the highest.

beats.scene: A hand-lettered sign says Student price beside a tray of small plants
beats.summary: An open discount for a group with less money can be fair and good for business.

beats.scene: A coin jar stands beside seedlings under a Pay what you like sign
beats.summary: Ines tries pay-what-you-like for seedlings, knowing studies give mixed results.

beats.scene: Ines counts coins from a jar while Theo reads the tally aloud
beats.summary: Some paid more and many paid little, so the idea suits special days, not a living.

beats.scene: Theo draws two columns headed Week one and Week two in a notebook
beats.summary: Ines and Theo plan a fair test: change one thing at a time and keep a record.

beats.scene: Ines compares two columns of numbers in the notebook with a smile
beats.summary: A small price rise on lavender slightly lowers sales but raises her income.

beats.scene: Ines chats with a customer while Theo counts sales on his fingers
beats.summary: What people say they will pay differs from what they do, so watch their behaviour.

beats.scene: A small sign reading Only three left stands beside a tray of spotted plants
beats.summary: Real scarcity raises value, but a false shortage is a trick.

beats.scene: A customer holds a small plant close and smells its leaves
beats.summary: People value what they hold more: the endowment effect.

beats.scene: Theo hesitates at a shop window full of crossed-out prices
beats.summary: Theo sees the same price tricks in shops and nearly falls for one himself.

beats.scene: Theo writes three questions on the back of a price card
beats.summary: Theo's three questions help any buyer, and Ines finds they help sellers too.

beats.scene: A customer walks away from the stall, then returns the next Saturday
beats.summary: Waiting a day cools impulse, and customers who return are happier.

beats.scene: Ines photographs a plant beside a phone showing her new online shop
beats.summary: Online, prices are compared in seconds, so honest photos and stories matter.

beats.scene: A box holding a small plant and a care card, ready to post
beats.summary: A monthly plant box gives steady income, and cancelling must be easy.

beats.scene: An orchid in full bloom on a sunny windowsill
beats.summary: Spreading a price over a plant's long life shows its value, if it is true.

beats.scene: Ines and Theo read a full notebook at a kitchen table with tea
beats.summary: After a year, Ines and Theo review what has really worked.

beats.scene: Ines writes tidy new price cards in clear round numbers
beats.summary: Her new cards are clear, honest and based on what she has learned.

beats.scene: Ines smiles behind a busy stall at sunrise, with customers queuing
beats.summary: The stall earns more and Ines worries less, though the puzzle is not solved.

beats.scene: Theo writes a sentence in large letters on the last notebook page
beats.summary: Theo sums it up: a price is a small story that the buyer tells themselves.

beats.scene: Ines pins a short list of five rules to the post of the stall
beats.summary: Ines pins her five rules: tell the truth, show the whole price, test one thing, be fair, help people choose.

beats.scene: Ines and Theo fold up the stall at sunset, smiling
beats.summary: There is no perfect price, only honest ones that cover costs, respect customers and are tested.

B1B2: Ines sells plants from a small stall at the Saturday market, and she loves her work. There is only one thing that keeps her awake at night, and that is the price cards.
Her nephew Theo helps at the stall on Saturdays, and he is full of questions. Today he holds up a card and asks how she chose the number.
Theo tells her that a price is more than a number, because it also sends a message. They decide to spend the year finding out how people really think about prices.
Most customers have no idea what a plant is really worth. Instead, they judge a price by comparing it with other things that they can see.

Psychologists call this pull an anchor: the first number we see drags our sense of a fair price towards it. Ines puts a tall palm marked 60 at the front, and her medium plants at 25 suddenly look cheap.
Some studies suggest that even experts, such as people who value houses for a living, are pulled by the asking price. Nobody is completely safe from an anchor, even when they know that it is there.
Ines wonders whether an anchor is a trick played on her customers. She decides that the big palm must be a really fine plant at a fair price, one that she would be happy to sell.
Ines sells mint in three pot sizes, small, medium and large. Most customers pick the middle one, because it feels safe, neither too small nor too expensive.

One Saturday she adds a medium basil pot at 13, only one dollar less than the large pot at 14. Almost nobody buys it, but more people than usual choose the large pot, because it now looks like a much better deal.
Ines thinks about it for a week and decides that she does not want to trick anyone. She will keep every choice honest, and she will use these ideas only to help people choose well.
Next, Ines tries giving away a free packet of seeds with each plant. People smile, and they seem far happier than a small discount would have made them.

A table of free plant cuttings draws a crowd, but most people walk away without buying anything. Ines learns that free can bring people closer, though it is useful only when it leads to something good.
For years Ines took only cash, but now she buys a small card machine. Researchers have often found that paying by card hurts less than handing over notes, so people tend to spend a little more.
A woman arrives with a gift card and happily buys the most beautiful plant on the stall. Theo explains that people keep mental boxes for their money, and that gift money feels lighter than wages.
A man asks for five dollars off a plant that costs 20, but he does not ask for the same on a tree that costs 300. The saving is exactly the same, yet it feels large in one case and tiny in the other.

She begins to sell three small herb pots together as a set, at a price a little lower than buying them one by one. Customers feel that they are making one easy choice instead of three separate payments.
Ines also makes gift sets, with a plant, a bag of soil and a care card in a paper bag. People gladly pay more for something that is ready to give, because it saves them time and thought.
Ines sells her own plant food for only three dollars, and nobody wants it. When she raises the price to six, it starts to sell, because people cannot test it and they use the price to judge it.

Many shoppers read the first digit of a price most carefully, so 19 can feel much cheaper than 20. Studies often find that such prices raise sales, although they can also make a product look less special.

Round numbers like 30 or 50 feel smooth and calm, so they suit things that people buy with their hearts. Exact numbers like 27 feel more like careful sums, and they suit things that people buy for use.

A card that says “was 30, now 24” works because the old price becomes a reference. Ines uses it only when 30 was really her price, because false sale prices are unfair and are against the law in many places.

Losses hurt more than equal gains please us, and researchers think that the sting is often about twice as strong. So when Ines wants to cover her card costs, she offers a small cash discount instead of adding a fee.
Ines has forty kinds of plant on one table, and many people stand there looking confused. Some studies suggest that too many choices can freeze us, although the effect is not found every time.
For each kind of plant, she now offers a small, medium and large size with a clear difference between them. Customers know at once which one suits their home and their wallet.

Ines is tempted to raise the price of her watering cans in the hot weather. Theo reminds her that people judge prices by fairness, and a price that feels like taking advantage can lose a customer for good.
The clay pots that she buys have become more expensive, so Ines must raise some of her prices. She pins a short, friendly note to the stall to explain why, and most customers understand.

Ines now delivers big plants to people's homes, and she shows the full price from the start, including delivery. Theo says that online shops often add fees at the last step, and that it makes buyers feel tricked.
Mrs Dale has bought plants from Ines for years, and she never checks the price. Ines realises that trust is the best thing a price can build, and that clever tricks could easily break it.
Ines writes down what each plant costs her: the pot, the soil, the fuel for her van and her own working hours. She discovers that two of her cheapest plants earn almost nothing at all.
Ines grows a rare spotted plant that collectors love, and she has priced it at what it cost her plus a little. A collector tells her gently that it is worth far more to people like him.
Many students in town have little money but love plants for their rooms. Ines offers an open discount on her small plants to anyone with a student card, and the sign is clear for everyone to read.
One Saturday, Ines lets customers pay whatever they like for her tiny seedlings. Studies of this idea give mixed results, so she watches carefully to see what happens at her own stall.
Some customers pay more than the usual price, especially people who know her, but many pay very little. At the end of the day the total is lower than normal, so Ines will not make it a habit.
Theo explains that if you change three things at once, you will never know which one made the difference. Together they plan a simple test of one change, two weeks and a tally on paper.
She raises the price of her lavender from six dollars to eight. She sells a few fewer plants, but she earns more money in total, so she keeps the new price.
When Ines asks customers what price they would pay, their answers are polite and not very useful. What people actually do at the stall is a much better guide than what they say.
When something is truly rare or nearly gone, people want it more, and Ines can say so honestly. She never invents a shortage, because a false “only two left” is a trick that customers soon notice.

Ines notices that once people hold a plant or smell its leaves, they are less willing to put it down. Psychologists call this the endowment effect, because things we own, or nearly own, feel more valuable.
Theo notices the same tricks in the shops in town: crossed-out prices, middle-sized choices and prices that end in nine. He laughs when he catches himself nearly falling for one.
He asks three questions before buying: what would I pay if I saw no other price, do I need it, and is the comparison real? Ines pins the list up near her cash box.
Theo's best advice for buyers is simple: wait one day before any big purchase. Ines sometimes tells a hesitant customer that the plant will still be there next Saturday, and many of them return.
Ines puts her best plants on a small online shop, where customers can compare prices in seconds. She cannot win by being the cheapest, so she shows good photos and tells the story of each plant.
Ines begins a monthly box with one small plant and a care card, for a fixed price. People like knowing the cost in advance, and Ines promises to make cancelling as easy as joining.

A well-cared-for orchid can live for many years, so Ines explains that a 36-dollar plant costs only a little each year. She says this only when it is true, because stretching a number is another kind of trick.
A year has passed, and the notebook is full of tallies, small tests and notes. Ines and Theo sit at the kitchen table and read it to see what they have really learned.
Her new cards are clear and tidy, with three sizes, honest anchors and a short note about each plant. She uses round numbers for gifts and prices like 19 for everyday plants.
By the end of the year the stall earns more, and Ines no longer lies awake thinking about prices. She still makes mistakes sometimes, but now she knows how to learn from them.
On the last page Theo writes one sentence in large letters: a price is a small story that a buyer tells themselves. Ines reads it twice and smiles, because it is exactly right.
Ines pins her rules to the post: tell the truth, show the whole price, test one change, be fair and help people choose. The rules are short, but she says that they took a year to learn.
As the sun goes down, Ines folds up the stall and thinks about the year. There is no perfect price, only honest ones that cover your costs, respect your customers and are tested against real life.
C1C2: Every Saturday before sunrise, Ines carries trays of green plants to her stall at the town market and arranges them in neat rows, with a small white card beside each one. She loves the smell of the soil and the pleasure of sending a plant home with someone who will care for it. What she does not love, however, is the card, because every price on it was a guess that she has never been able to check.

Her nephew Theo, who is 16 and studies psychology at school, helps at the stall on Saturdays and asks questions about everything. This morning he holds up a card and wants to know how she decided that a medium fern should cost 25 dollars. Ines laughs, then admits, a little embarrassed, that she chose the number because it felt right.

A price is not only a number, Theo says, but also a message, and the buyer reads that message in a fraction of a second. Ines, who had always thought of her cards as simple labels, begins to suspect that they have been talking to her customers all along. They agree to spend the coming year watching, testing and reading, and to write down everything that they learn.

Very few customers arrive knowing what a pot of lavender ought to cost, because nobody keeps such numbers in their head. Instead, the mind searches for something to compare it with, and it will use almost anything that happens to be nearby, whether that is fair or not. That one habit, Theo says, is the key to the whole puzzle, and it is the thread that they will follow all year.

Psychologists call it anchoring: the first number we meet quietly pulls our sense of a fair price towards itself, even when that number has nothing to do with the thing we want. Ines places a tall palm tree, marked 60, at the very front of her stall, and the medium plants behind it, at 25, begin to look like bargains. The effect is real and well studied, Theo warns, but it is not magic, and a number that is plainly absurd will only make people laugh.

Researchers have found that even trained professionals, such as people whose job is to value houses, tend to be nudged by the asking price that they are shown first. The result does not mean that these people are foolish, only that the mind uses the nearest number as a place to begin. Knowing about anchors helps a little, Theo says, but it does not make anyone immune.

Ines wonders, for a moment, whether using an anchor is a clever way of cheating the people who trust her. She decides that the line is honesty: the palm must be a truly splendid plant at a price that she could defend, and she must be glad if someone buys it. An anchor that tells the truth helps customers to see the range of their choices, while a false one only borrows their trust.

Ines sells mint in three pot sizes, and she notices that most people reach for the middle one, as if the choice had been made for them. Researchers call this the compromise effect: when we are unsure, the middle option feels like the safest and most sensible answer. It is not a rule, Theo adds, but it is common enough that the order and spacing of choices matter more than most sellers realise.

For her basil she has always sold a small pot at 8 and a large pot at 14, but one Saturday she adds a medium pot at 13, and Theo keeps a tally on the back of a card. Almost nobody buys the medium pot, yet more people than usual choose the large one, because next to such a poor offer it looks like an obvious bargain. Researchers call this the decoy effect; it is well known, but it appears mainly when options are hard to compare, and it does not work every time.

The decoy troubles Ines, because she can see how easily such a trick could slide into something unkind. After thinking about it for a week, she decides that every pot she sells must be a real choice, with a size and a price that make sense on their own. Her rule becomes simple: use what you learn to help people choose, and never to catch them out.

Next, Ines puts a basket of seed packets by her cash box and gives one away free with every plant. The customers smile as though they had been handed a present, and Theo explains that a price of zero feels different from any other price, not merely a little lower. Studies suggest that people will often take a free item that they hardly want, simply because it costs nothing.

When Ines sets out a table of free plant cuttings, a crowd gathers within minutes, but most of the people drift away again with nothing but a green leaf in a paper cup. She learns that free is excellent at attracting attention and poor at creating loyalty, unless it leads naturally to something that people truly value. A free gift should be a doorway, Theo says, and not a dead end.

For years Ines accepted only cash, until a customer asked whether she had a card machine, and she finally bought one. Psychologists have often found that parting with paper money is more painful than tapping a card, which is why shoppers who pay electronically tend to spend somewhat more. The lesson, Theo points out, is that the pain of paying is real, and that sellers can make it lighter or heavier without changing a single price.

A woman arrives with a gift card, and without a moment's hesitation she chooses the most beautiful and expensive orchid on the stall. Theo explains that people keep invisible boxes in their minds, labelled rent, food, savings and treats, and that money in the treat box is spent far more freely than money in the rent box. The coins are identical, but the feelings that surround them are not.

A man asks for five dollars off a 20-dollar plant, then, a few minutes later, shrugs when she cannot lower the price of a 300-dollar tree by the same amount. Five dollars is five dollars, yet the mind does not measure it that way, for it compares the saving with the price, so the same sum feels huge in one case and tiny in the other. Ines decides that her small discounts will go on her small items, where they will be noticed.

She begins to sell three small herb pots together as a set, at a price a little lower than buying them one by one. Customers seem to feel that they are making a single easy decision rather than three separate payments, and many who came for one pot leave with three. A bundle works best, Theo notes, when the things in it truly belong together.

Ines also begins to make gift sets, each holding a plant, a small bag of good soil and a handwritten care card, tied up in brown paper. Customers happily pay more for such a set than for its parts, because what they are buying is not only the plant but also the saved time, the thought and the pleasure of giving. A price, Theo realises, is partly a payment for convenience, and a good seller is paid for solving a small problem as well as for selling a plant.

Ines bottles her own plant food and prices it at three dollars, yet it sits on the table all morning while customers glance at it and move on. When she raises the price to six, sales begin, because buyers cannot easily test a liquid and so they read the price as a clue to its quality. This does not always happen, Theo cautions, and a high price must always be backed by something real.

Many shoppers read the left-hand digit of a price most carefully, which is why 19 can feel noticeably cheaper than 20, even though the gap is a single dollar. Studies often find that such prices raise sales, but they can also make a product seem more ordinary, so they suit everyday goods better than luxuries. Ines decides to use them on her small plants and to keep round numbers for her gifts.

Round numbers such as 30 or 50 feel smooth and effortless, which makes them a natural fit for things that people buy with their hearts, like gifts and flowers. Exact numbers such as 27 feel like the result of a calculation, and they tend to suit goods that people buy with their heads. The idea is subtle, and the evidence is mixed, so Ines treats it as a suggestion to test rather than a law.

A card that says “was 30, now 24” works because the old price becomes a reference point, and the lower number feels like a gain. Ines uses it only when 30 was truly her price for some weeks, because a made-up “was” price is a deception, and in many places it is against the law. Honest sales, she tells Theo, can be just as exciting as dishonest ones, and they do not cost her a customer's trust or her own peace of mind.

Psychologists have found that a loss tends to hurt more than an equal gain pleases, with the sting often estimated at roughly twice the pleasure. When Ines wants to cover the cost of her card machine, she therefore offers a small discount for cash instead of charging a fee for cards, although the sums come out almost exactly the same. The words around a price, Theo says, can change how it feels without changing what it is.

Ines has forty kinds of plant crowded on one long table, and she notices that many visitors stand in front of it for a long time and then walk away. Some studies suggest that too many options can overwhelm a shopper, though other studies have not found the effect, so it is better seen as a risk than as a law. She trims the table to a dozen of her best plants, and the choosing becomes easier.

For each kind of plant, Ines now offers a small, a medium and a large size, with a clear and visible difference between them. Customers can see at a glance which one suits their windowsill and which suits their wallet, and nobody has to guess what the extra money buys. Clarity, she finds, is often more persuasive than cleverness, and it is certainly a great deal more comfortable for everyone involved.

A hot week arrives, and suddenly everyone wants a watering can, so Ines is tempted to raise the price. Theo reminds her that people judge prices by fairness as well as by logic, and experiments show that they will even refuse a free but unequal share in order to punish someone who seems greedy. She keeps her price where it is, and she remembers the people who thank her.

When her supplier raises the cost of the clay pots, Ines has no choice but to raise some of her own prices a little. She pins a short, friendly note to the stall that explains the reason, and she is relieved to find that most customers accept it with a nod. People forgive a price rise that has a clear and fair explanation far more easily than one that arrives in silence.

Ines now delivers large plants to people's homes, and she shows the full price, delivery included, from the very first moment. Theo has seen online shops reveal extra fees only at the last step of a purchase, and he says that the practice leaves buyers feeling tricked, even when the total is fair. In some places the rules now require sellers to show the full price at the start.

Mrs Dale, an elderly regular in a green coat, has bought plants from Ines for years and has never once checked a price card. Ines realises that this quiet trust is worth more than any clever trick, because a customer who believes that prices are fair will return week after week. Tricks may win one sale on a busy morning, but honesty, repeated patiently for years, can win a hundred more.

One evening Ines writes down everything that each plant costs her: the seed, the pot, the soil, the fuel for her van, the market fee and the hours of her own work. She is startled to discover that two of her cheapest and most popular plants earn her almost nothing once her time is counted. Psychology can help a price to feel right, Theo says, but arithmetic must first make sure that it is possible.

Ines grows a rare spotted plant that takes two years to mature, and she has priced it at roughly what it cost her plus a little extra. A collector who has searched for it for months tells her gently that, to someone like him, it is worth much more than that. Costs set the lowest sensible price, Theo concludes, but the highest one is set by what the plant is worth to the person who wants it.

Many of the students who walk through the market have little money but a great wish to bring some green into their rooms. Ines offers a small, open discount on her smallest plants to anyone with a student card, and she paints the offer on a sign so that nobody can feel that someone else is being treated better in secret. A fair price offered openly, she finds, builds goodwill instead of resentment, and the students tell their friends about the stall.

On one Saturday morning, Ines tries something bold and lets customers pay whatever they like for her tiny seedlings. Studies of such schemes have given mixed results, since some buyers pay generously and others pay almost nothing, so she treats the day as an experiment and watches closely. Theo writes down every sale, and he promises not to guess about the result.

A few customers, mostly people who know her, pay more than her usual price, but many others pay very little, and by the end of the day the jar holds less than it normally does. Ines decides that the idea is lovely for a special occasion and unwise as a way to earn a living. The lesson, Theo says, is that an experiment has done its job when it teaches you something, even if the answer is no.

If you change three things at once, Theo explains, you will never know which of them made the difference, and so you will learn nothing and may even draw the wrong conclusion. Together they plan a simple test: one change, two weeks at the old price and two weeks at the new one, with every sale written in a notebook. Weather, holidays and the mood of the crowd will always muddy the result a little, but a careful record is far better than a feeling.

Following their plan, Ines raises the price of her lavender from six dollars to eight and watches the tally for two weeks. She sells a few fewer plants than before, but the extra two dollars on every plant more than makes up for the loss, so she keeps the new price. Another change, a higher price on her fern, brings the opposite result, and she quietly sets it back.

When Ines asks her customers what price they would be willing to pay, the answers are polite, rounded and not very useful, because people find it hard to predict their own behaviour. Watching what they actually do at the stall, and counting it, turns out to be a far better guide than listening to what they say. Questions are still worth asking, Theo adds, because people often explain their reasons well, but behaviour is the final judge of whether a price works.

When something is truly rare or nearly sold out, people value it more, so Ines is happy to tell customers that only three of the spotted plants remain today. She never invents a shortage, because a false “last one” is a deception that people soon notice, and a deception costs far more than a single sale. Scarcity, like an anchor, is a fair tool only when it is true, and a good seller never has to pretend about it.

Ines notices that once a customer has picked up a plant, touched its leaves and smelt its scent, it becomes much harder for them to put it down again. Psychologists call this the endowment effect, the tendency to value what we already hold, or feel that we nearly hold, more than something we have never touched. She stops telling people to look but not touch, and she invites them to take a plant in their hands.

Walking home one afternoon, Theo spots the same patterns in every shop window: crossed-out prices, three-size menus, giant numbers on bright signs and prices that end in nine. He laughs when he catches himself nearly buying a jacket that he does not need, because it was marked down from a high price that he had never actually seen anyone pay. Knowing the tricks, he says, makes them easier to see, but it does not make them disappear, and it certainly does not make every bargain safe.

Theo writes three questions on the back of a price card, to ask before he buys anything. What would I pay if I saw no other price, he asks; do I truly need this; and is the comparison that I am looking at a real one? Ines copies them onto a card for the stall and, to her surprise, finds that they help her as a seller as much as they help her as a buyer.

Theo's most practical advice for any buyer is to wait a day before any purchase that matters, because the excitement of a bargain fades quickly, while real need does not. Ines sometimes tells a hesitant customer that the plant will still be waiting next Saturday, and a surprising number return, happier and more certain than before. Selling that way, she says, costs her a few quick sales and earns her many lasting customers.

Ines puts her best plants into a small online shop, where customers can compare dozens of prices in a few seconds. She cannot hope to win by being the cheapest, so she competes in other ways: with honest photographs, careful descriptions and the story of how each plant was grown. A price, she learns, is rarely judged alone, and the things around it often decide the result.

Ines begins a monthly box, which carries one small plant and a care card to a customer's door for a fixed price. People enjoy knowing the cost in advance and being surprised by the plant, and Ines enjoys the steady income, but she insists that cancelling must be as easy as joining. Many companies profit from customers who forget that they are paying, she says, and she does not want to be one of them.

A well-cared-for orchid can live for many years and flower again and again, so Ines tells her customers that a 36-dollar plant costs only a few dollars for each year of pleasure. She is careful to say this only when it is true, and to explain how the plant must be looked after, because spreading a cost over time is fair only when the benefit is real. Honest framing, she thinks, is simply telling the whole story of a price, including the care and the patience that a good plant needs.

A year has passed since Theo first asked his question, and the notebook is now thick with tallies, tiny experiments and crossed-out guesses. Ines and Theo sit at the kitchen table with a pot of tea and read it from the first page to the last, hunting for the lessons that have held up. Some of their favourite ideas, they notice, worked only once, and a few ordinary ones worked every time.

Her new price cards are tidy and clear, with three sizes for each plant, one honest anchor at the front and a short sentence about the care that each plant needs. She uses round numbers for gifts and prices such as 19 for everyday plants, and she writes the real reason whenever a price has changed. Nothing on them is a trick, and, to her delight, nothing on them needs to be.

By the end of the year, the stall earns noticeably more than before, and Ines no longer lies awake at night worrying about her price cards. She still makes mistakes now and then, but she knows how to test, how to listen and how to correct herself, and that confidence is worth more than any perfect number. The puzzle, she admits with a smile, has not been completely solved, and she suspects that it never will be.

On the last page of the notebook, Theo writes a single sentence in large letters: a price is a small story that the buyer tells themselves about value, fairness and trust. Ines reads it twice, then a third time, and decides that it explains almost everything that they have discovered during the year. A seller who understands that story, she thinks, has a duty to tell it truthfully.

Ines pins her five rules to the post of the stall, where every customer can read them: tell the truth, show the whole price, test one change at a time, treat everyone fairly, and help people to choose well. They are short enough to fit on a card, but they took a whole year, a nephew and a notebook to learn. Some customers stop to read them, and a few ask whether they can borrow the idea.

As the sun sinks behind the market hall, Ines folds her tables and thinks about everything that a year of small questions has taught her. There is no perfect price, only prices that cover the cost of the work, respect the customer who reads them and have been tested against real life rather than imagined. If you remember one thing, Theo says as he lifts the last crate, remember that every number is also a message, so make sure that yours is a kind one.
